decision:mlm-and-seminars.question: How much money do MLM participants actually make?
decision:mlm-and-seminars.title: How Much Money Do MLM Participants Actually Make?
alternates: Can You Really Get Rich Recruiting People Into an MLM?
What MLM Income Disclosures Admit in the Fine Print
decision:mlm-and-seminars.whyWatch: Everyone has been pitched by a friend. The companies' own income disclosures, a nationally representative survey and a 30-company analysis all say the same thing, and the pitch's central promise, leveraged income from a downline, is where the numbers are most revealing.
decision:mlm-and-seminars.tension: The pitch sells leverage: recruit and earn from everyone below you. The disclosures show the leverage is real for a fraction of a percent and the structure guarantees most people sit at the bottom.
decision:mlm-and-seminars.evidenceNeeded: Income distributions for participants net of expenses, and evidence on whether income comes from recruiting or retail sales.
decision:mlm-and-seminars.premise: Four independent documents answer the question the same way, each with a limit the video must state. AARP's 2018 probability sample of 601 participants found 47% lost money and 25% made any profit, self-reported. The FTC's 2024 review of 70 income disclosures found most participants made $1,000 or less a year, before expenses. Taylor's analysis of 30 companies gets to 99.6% losing money only after subtracting required purchases, so that figure depends on his method. The downline promise is structurally true (the pay plans do route income from recruits) and practically false for almost everyone: in rank tables over 90% sit in the lowest cohort averaging under $100. The exhaustion arithmetic is illustrated by Taylor, not tested by any study.

arc.hook: A friend's message: join under me, build a team, earn while you sleep. How much do people in that position actually make?
arc.conflict: The companies publish income disclosures. Read one aloud: median earnings, share with zero income, and what the fine print says is not deducted.
arc.evidence: AARP's survey (47% lost money), the FTC's 70-disclosure review (most under $1,000 a year before expenses), Taylor's 30-company analysis (99.6% lose after required purchases, by his method), and the rank tables showing where the downline income goes.
arc.resolution: The leverage exists, for the top fraction of a percent, because the plans pay for recruiting rather than retail; most participants are structurally at the bottom.
arc.takeaway: Ask for the income disclosure before joining, read the expense fine print, and treat 'leveraged income' as the company's revenue model rather than yours.

decision:mlm-and-seminars.audience: General YouTube viewers who have been pitched an MLM by a friend or seen one promoted online; no knowledge of compensation plans, surveys or regulators assumed.

contradicted:network-marketing-success-l.question: Is MLM success a skill you can learn, or a matter of when you joined?
contradicted:network-marketing-success-l.title: Is MLM Success a Skill, or Just Being Early?
alternates: Why the Top of an MLM Is Full of People Who Joined First
Can Training Really Make You an MLM Winner?
contradicted:network-marketing-success-l.whyWatch: Every MLM sells training on the premise that success is learnable. If position in the chain decides outcomes, the training is a fee for a lottery ticket.
contradicted:network-marketing-success-l.tension: The industry says skill; the one court finding in the corpus says seniority.
contradicted:network-marketing-success-l.evidenceNeeded: Earnings related to join date and to training received, within the same company.

Unblocked by company or regulator data relating MLM earnings to join date or to training received across distributors (e.g. tenure-cohort income disclosures, or a court or FTC analysis of distributor records).

coherence.reason: One question, whether most people who day trade lose and whether anyone beats the odds, answered by the base rate, the size of the profitable minority, the HFT explanation and the effect of trading frequency. Options strategies and sports betting are different markets with their own evidence and are dropped.

decision:trading-and-betting.question: Do most people who day trade lose money, and can anyone beat the odds?
decision:trading-and-betting.title: Do 97% of Day Traders Really Lose Money?
alternates: Can Anyone Make a Living Day Trading?
What Happens to People Who Day Trade for a Year
decision:trading-and-betting.whyWatch: Sixteen sources in the corpus say most day traders lose, and the pitch videos say a disciplined strategy beats that. Two complete-market datasets, Brazil and Taiwan, let the viewer see the whole distribution, including the winners.
decision:trading-and-betting.tension: The pitch: discipline and a proven strategy make you consistently profitable. The data: a small minority is predictably profitable, and the longer people trade the smaller their chance of being in it.
decision:trading-and-betting.evidenceNeeded: Complete trading records for a population of day traders over at least a year, net of fees, with the share who profit and whether it rises with experience.
decision:trading-and-betting.premise: The Brazilian study followed 1,551 people who day traded index futures for more than 300 days: 97% lost money net of fees, and the share with a positive result fell with every extra day traded. The Taiwan study covers every day trader on the exchange from 1992 to 2006 and finds reliably negative returns before and after costs. Both find a small, predictably profitable minority (under 3%), which is the honest form of the 'disciplined strategy' claim. Limits the video must carry: Brazil is index futures and Taiwan is stocks in an earlier era; the HFT finding is from futures; the EU CFD figures are a different product; and nothing here measures momentum-stock traders, so the claim that an expert can multiply an account in a month is unchecked rather than refuted.

arc.hook: A screenshot of a small account turned into a large one in a month. How often does that happen to people who try?
arc.conflict: The sources promise consistency with discipline; the regulators and academics who can see every account say most lose.
arc.evidence: Brazil: 1,551 persistent traders, 97% lost, the best averaged US$310 a day with a standard deviation of US$2,560. Taiwan: every trader on the exchange, losses before and after costs in every year but one. Both: a predictably profitable minority under 3%, and no learning curve.
arc.resolution: Day trading is possible to win at and overwhelmingly lost at; frequency and fees erode results, and retail traders face algorithms with a structural edge. The evidence does not touch the exceptional-month story, so say so.
arc.takeaway: Treat day trading as an expensive hobby with a small chance of being in the 3%, and treat any strategy sold as consistent as a claim its seller must prove with audited records.

contradicted:experienced-day-trader-can-.question: Can an experienced day trader really multiply a small account in a month?
contradicted:experienced-day-trader-can-.title: Can a Skilled Day Trader Really Multiply a Small Account in a Month?
alternates: The Momentum-Trading Promise, Checked Against the Data
What the Best Day Traders Actually Made
contradicted:experienced-day-trader-can-.whyWatch: This is the specific promise in the pitch videos, and it is the one the base-rate studies cannot answer directly.
contradicted:experienced-day-trader-can-.tension: A possibility claim against population data: the best day traders on record earn a small daily edge on average, which shows how rare large gains are, not that they are impossible.
contradicted:experienced-day-trader-can-.evidenceNeeded: Audited account histories of momentum-stock day traders, or the distribution of monthly account growth across a population of them.
contradicted:experienced-day-trader-can-.research: The corpus has base-rate studies of Brazilian futures day traders and Taiwan stock day traders, including the persistently skilled top 500 (28.1 bps a day after fees on average); group averages cannot rule out an individual momentum trader multiplying an account in a month. It needs audited account histories of momentum-stock day traders or a study of the distribution of monthly account growth (the top tail, with leverage) across such a population.

contradicted:beginners-experience-can-ma.tension: A possibility claim against one enforcement case and one trial in which the AI helped only the owners who were already doing well.
contradicted:beginners-experience-can-ma.evidenceNeeded: Outcomes for a sample of beginners across AI side hustles, not one firm's customers.

conflict:commission-free-brokerage-incre.reject: folded into surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-order-flow: the trading boom is the second act of the commission-free story

coherence.reason: One question, whether zero-commission trading is free, answered by who pays the broker (order flow), where the cost reappears (spreads, especially on options) and what free trading did to trading volume.

surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-or.question: Is commission-free trading actually free?
surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-or.title: Is 'Commission-Free' Trading Actually Free?
alternates: Who Pays When Your Broker Charges Nothing?
The Hidden Cost Inside Zero-Commission Trades
surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-or.whyWatch: Most retail traders use a zero-commission app. The paper on retail options trading puts a number on what they pay instead, and it is larger than the commissions were.
surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-or.tension: 'Free' on the screen; in options, a 12.3% average quoted spread on the weekly contracts retail prefers, and market makers who pay for the flow giving worse prices.
surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-or.evidenceNeeded: Measured payment for order flow and effective spreads paid by retail, and evidence on whether removing commissions changed how much people trade.
surprise:commission-free-brokers-sell-or.premise: Commission-free brokers are paid for order flow: wholesalers pay the brokerage for the retail orders routed to them (Bryzgalova and colleagues count $284.4m for stock orders and $581.2m for options in the second quarter of 2021). Whether that leaves the trader with a hidden cost depends on the asset, and the video must say so. Ernst and Spatt find that in stocks wholesaler routing benefits retail traders with smaller spreads than the exchanges, so for ordinary stock trades the evidence does not show a hidden cost from order flow; in options it harms them, with PFOF-paying market makers causally associated with wider spreads. Options are also where the spreads are: the average quoted spread on S&P 500 stock options is 17.2%, and half the wholesaler trades in the Bryzgalova sample are options with under a week to expiry at a 12.3% average spread, costs the paper says are masked by zero commissions. The paper's dollar totals ($4.13bn of spread costs against about $800m of commissions) sit in lines no verdict cites yet, so the script either asks for them through record-sources or leaves them out. The evidence is US markets. The boom is descriptive, not causal: the same paper and the Brazilian study link zero commissions to a surge in retail and day trading, while an eToro test found no change in one narrow measure of trading behaviour after commissions were removed. The video should present that as a limit on the boom claim, not on the cost claim.

arc.hook: Your trade cost nothing. Someone paid your broker for it. What did you pay?
arc.conflict: Free trading was sold as democratising markets; the evidence says the cost moved rather than vanished for options, the product retail likes best, while stock orders routed for payment got better prices than the exchanges offered.
arc.evidence: Payment for order flow, the split between stocks (better prices) and options (wider spreads from paying market makers), quoted spreads on options versus stocks, and the post-2019 surge in retail and options volume, with the eToro null result as the caveat.
arc.resolution: Free is a pricing model: for stock trades the order-flow deal did not cost retail on price, but in options the cost reappears as wide spreads, heaviest on short-dated contracts.
arc.takeaway: Count the spread, not the commission, and be most careful with the products the app makes easiest to trade.

coherence.reason: One question, whether buyers or sellers make the money from money-making courses, answered by what the sellers earned, what buyers ended up with, how the earnings figures are presented, and how the funnel and financing work. The rented-lifestyle claim is a side point with no evidence and is dropped.

decision:who-makes-the-money.question: Who actually makes money from get-rich-quick courses: the buyers or the sellers?
decision:who-makes-the-money.title: Who Really Gets Rich From Get-Rich-Quick Courses?
alternates: The Business Model Behind 'Passive Income' Courses
What FTC Complaints Say About Guru Courses
decision:who-makes-the-money.whyWatch: Twenty-five sources in the corpus say the seller earns more from the course than from the method. Three FTC cases open the books on how that works, from the free seminar to the credit-card application.
decision:who-makes-the-money.tension: The pitch shows the method's income; the complaints show the sellers' income came from the pitch.
decision:who-makes-the-money.evidenceNeeded: Sellers' revenue by source, buyers' net outcomes, and how advertised figures relate to net earnings.
decision:who-makes-the-money.premise: The evidence is two FTC enforcement actions (Automators/Empire and Nudge), which are allegations and settlements about two firms, not a survey of courses in general, plus the FTC's review of MLM income disclosures for the gross-not-net pattern; the video must say so in those words. Within that limit the pattern is consistent: over $7 million of buyer payments flowed to Empire's founders, whose documented income came from selling the opportunity; most buyers did not recoup their fees and virtually none earned the advertised amounts; advertised figures were gross sales while clients lost money net of fees, inventory and interest; the founder's results were conceded in fine print to be atypical; buyers were steered into $15,000 to $80,000 of business credit for working capital (inventory, not the package fee); and Nudge's free seminar was a pitch for a $1,100 workshop that pitched $40,000 training. Nothing here shows edited screenshots.

arc.hook: The free seminar, the $1,100 workshop, the $40,000 'advanced training': walk through one funnel the FTC documented.
arc.conflict: Buyers were shown the method's income; the complaints trace where the money actually went.
arc.evidence: The Automators complaint (founders' income, buyers' outcomes, gross-versus-net figures, fine print, financing), the Nudge funnel, and the FTC's finding that no MLM income disclosure nets out expenses.
arc.resolution: In the documented cases the course was the business and the buyers were the revenue; whether that generalises is the open question.
arc.takeaway: Ask what the seller's income is from, insist on net figures for typical buyers, and never finance a course on credit.

surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.question: Do most new businesses really fail within a few years?
surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.title: Do Most New Businesses Really Fail in a Few Years?
alternates: How Long Does the Average New Business Actually Last?
The Survival Curve Behind 'Most Businesses Fail'
surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.whyWatch: The failure statistic is quoted both to discourage and to sell; the official survival table says something more precise.
surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.tension: 'Most fail within a few years' against a curve where half are still open after five.
surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.evidenceNeeded: Survival rates by age for new establishments, with a breakdown for online stores.
surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.premise: The BLS survival table says 79.6% of establishments opened in 2015 survived one year, 61.4% three, 50.2% five and 34.7% ten, so about half close within five years and two-thirds within ten. 'Most fail within a few years' overstates it; exits include sales and relocations, not only failures; and there is no breakdown for online stores. Taylor's second-hand SBA and NFIB figures agree on the shape.

arc.hook: Nine in ten businesses fail: where does that number come from?
arc.evidence: The BLS cohort survival curve, what an 'exit' includes, and the absence of online-store data.
arc.resolution: About half within five years, two-thirds within ten; 'most within a few years' is wrong, 'most eventually' is right.
arc.takeaway: Quote the curve, not the slogan.

surprise:most-new-businesses-including-o.chainWhy: Ordinary businesses survive far better than the 90-95% failure rate MLM promoters quote to make their opportunity look like the safer way to own a business (Taylor), so the next question is what MLM participants actually make.

coherence.reason: One mechanism (whether a stop fixes the loss on a leveraged position), two regulators' findings on it.

surprise:leverage-lets-small-account-tak.question: Does leverage really let you take a big position while keeping your risk fixed?
surprise:leverage-lets-small-account-tak.title: Does Leverage Really Keep Your Risk Fixed?
alternates: What Leverage Does to a Small Trading Account
Why 'Only Risk What You Put In' Isn't How Margin Works
surprise:leverage-lets-small-account-tak.whyWatch: The pitch says leverage lets a small account trade big with the downside capped at the stop; the EU and UK regulators say a stop cannot guarantee that.
surprise:leverage-lets-small-account-tak.tension: Fixed risk in the pitch; gapping, close-outs that come too late and losses beyond the deposit in the regulators' assessments.
surprise:leverage-lets-small-account-tak.evidenceNeeded: Regulatory or account-level evidence on how leverage changes the size and probability of losses for retail clients.
surprise:leverage-lets-small-account-tak.premise: Before checking, the best guess was "partly": sizing a leveraged position to a stop does set the planned loss, and in ordinary markets the realised loss is close to it. The EU regulator (ESMA, 2018) says leverage raises the chance of a larger loss more than of a larger gain, that automatic margin close-out reduces but does not eliminate the risk of losing all or more than the deposit, and that in a gap the trader may be unable to close at their price. The UK regulator (FCA, 2016) says even a mandatory close-out is not a guaranteed stop-loss: in volatile markets clients can lose their whole deposit or more. Both are regulators' assessments of retail CFDs, not measurements of how often or how far traders' own stop orders slip, so the evidence shows the risk is not fixed, not by how much it usually moves.

arc.hook: State the pitch: leverage lets a small account take a big position while the stop keeps the dollar risk fixed.
arc.resolution: A stop sets the planned loss, and in calm markets that is roughly what is lost; but in a gap or a fast market the position closes at the next available price, and the EU and UK regulators both say losses can then exceed the deposit, so the risk is capped only in ordinary conditions. Neither regulator measures how often stops slip, so the story says the cap is not guaranteed, not how large the overrun typically is.

decision:what-the-evidence-favours.reject: a list of consolation morals, not a question: compounding, passive income, luck, survivorship and equity each need their own evidence

coherence.reason: One question, why success stories mislead, with survivorship and the role of luck as its two halves.

conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.question: Why do get-rich-quick success stories sound so convincing?
conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.title: Why Do So Many Get-Rich-Quick Stories Sound Convincing?
alternates: Survivorship Bias: The Trick Behind Every Success Story
How Much of Getting Rich Is Luck?
conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.whyWatch: Thirteen sources make the survivorship argument; the corpus has a model of the mechanism and one large test of it, on companies rather than on the quickly rich.
conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.tension: A persuasive argument whose best measurement is about firms celebrated in success books, not about people who got rich quickly or anyone who followed their advice.
conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.evidenceNeeded: Outcomes for people who followed advice from the quickly rich, or a base-rate study of how individual fortunes are made.
conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.premise: Many sources say advice from people who got rich quickly is survivorship bias. The evidence supports the mechanism, in a narrower setting: a toy agent-based model shows how judging talent from success rates the luckiest as the most talented, and a screen of 53,038 listed firms over 1966-2008 finds sustained superior profitability in about 0.5% of firms, with only 9 of the 209 firms used as cases in nine popular success books beating their peers beyond chance. Both are about firms or simulated agents, not people who got rich quickly; no study here measures what happens to people who follow such advice, and the underestimation of luck is inferred, not measured.

arc.hook: Success stories are told by the people they worked for.
arc.conflict: Thirteen sources call the advice of the quickly rich survivorship bias; the advice-givers say they earned it.
arc.evidence: A toy model of talent and luck shows the mechanism; a screen of 53,038 firms finds that most companies celebrated in success books perform indistinguishably from luck (9 of 209 beat their peers), and that sustained superior profitability is rare (about 0.5% of firms).
arc.resolution: The survivorship mechanism is real and measurable for corporate success lessons; for individual get-rich-quick advice the evidence is by analogy, since no study here tracks people who followed it.
arc.takeaway: Before taking a success story as a method, ask how many people did the same thing and failed; the data on firms say the answer is usually most of them, though no one has measured it for the quickly rich.

conflict:advice-people-who-got-rich-quic.research: The evidence is a toy agent-based model (context) and a screen of 53,038 listed firms showing most companies in success books perform indistinguishably from luck (partial, 0.35): both bear on the mechanism by analogy, neither measures advice from people who got rich quickly. Unblocking needs a study of individuals: outcomes of people who followed the methods of the quickly rich against the full population who tried them (for example, a cohort of traders, sellers or founders who copied a publicised winner), or a base-rate study of how individual fortunes are made that separates luck from method.

coherence.reason: One question about one rhetorical move.

conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.question: Guru pitches trash the day job and the degree: do jobs and degrees actually pay?
conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.title: Do Day Jobs and Degrees Really Not Pay?
alternates: The Pitch Says Your Job Is a Trap. What the Earnings Data Say
Do Salaried Jobs and Degrees Pay Off? What the Pitch Leaves Out
conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.whyWatch: Many pitches open by insulting the viewer's job and degree; what jobs and degrees typically pay is checkable, even if the seller's motive is not.
conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.tension: The pitch's premise is that the safe path is a trap; the earnings data say the typical worker does better on it, with real exceptions.
conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.evidenceNeeded: Earnings by education and by employment type for the typical worker; the sales-tactic motive itself is not tested by any study here.
conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.premise: Whether trashing jobs and degrees is deliberately a sales tactic is not something these studies test; what they test is whether the paths being trashed pay. On average they do: over 1970-2013 US full-time workers with a bachelor's degree earned about 56 percent more than high school graduates (NY Fed), though part of that premium may reflect who goes to college and averages hide wide individual variation; the median self-employed person earns significantly less than they would as an employee, though the mean is sensitive to how earnings are measured and the spread is far wider (Hamilton 2000, as summarised by Moskowitz and Vissing-Jorgensen); and the best-paid business owners, the incorporated, are the most educated, drawn from high-earning salaried workers, while the unincorporated earn less than employees (Levine and Rubinstein).

arc.hook: Many get-rich pitches open the same way: your job is a trap and your degree was a waste.
arc.conflict: The pitch sells an escape from a path it says does not pay; the question is whether the path really does not pay, not what the seller intends, which no study here measures.
arc.evidence: Three sources: the NY Fed on the college wage premium over four decades (with its ability-selection and averages caveats); Hamilton's finding that the median self-employed earns less than as an employee (median, not mean); Levine and Rubinstein on who the high-earning business owners are.
arc.resolution: For the typical person both the degree and the salaried job pay more than the alternative the pitch offers; some individuals do better on their own, and the premium is partly who chooses each path.
arc.takeaway: An insult to your job is not evidence; ask what the median person on each path earns.

conflict:demeaning-salaried-jobs-college.research: Both earnings halves now have evidence (NY Fed college premium; Hamilton via Moskowitz and Vissing-Jorgensen on median self-employment earnings; Levine and Rubinstein), but each bears on only part of the claim and none tests the sales-tactic motive. Unblocking needs a content analysis or enforcement record showing that pitches which disparage jobs and degrees go on to sell a course or programme, or a single study at full strength on what the typical worker earns from a degree and a salaried job against self-employment.

coherence.reason: One question, whether dropshipping and faceless channels still pay, but the studies found bear only on the mechanism and on YouTube view counts, not on what people who try earn.

decision:selling-online.question: Can you still make money dropshipping or running a faceless channel?
decision:selling-online.title: Can You Still Make Money Dropshipping?
alternates: Why Online Side Hustles Stop Paying Once They Are Taught
Dropshipping and Faceless Channels: What Is Left for Latecomers?
decision:selling-online.whyWatch: The most-pitched schemes in the corpus, with a plausible mechanism (crowding) and no measurement of outcomes for people who try.
decision:selling-online.tension: A crowding argument everyone makes and no outcome data.
decision:selling-online.evidenceNeeded: Outcome data for a cohort of new dropshipping stores or faceless channels: survival, revenue, net of ad spend.
decision:selling-online.research: Still no outcome data: the NDSS 2024 dropshipping study only describes the no-inventory model, McLean and Pontiff 2016 shows published stock anomalies decay (an analogy for crowding, not consumer arbitrage), and McGrady et al. 2023 measures views across all YouTube uploads, not income of new or automation channels; nothing checks the paid-traffic margin claim. Unblock with a cohort of new dropshipping stores or faceless channels followed over a year (survival, revenue net of ad spend and goods), e.g. platform, payment-processor or tax data, or a study of ad costs and copycat entry for dropshipped products.

coherence.reason: One question about one product category.

conflict:retail-trading-bots-not-beat-ma.question: Do retail AI trading bots beat the market?
conflict:retail-trading-bots-not-beat-ma.title: Do AI Trading Bots Actually Beat the Market?
alternates: Can a Bot Trade Better Than You?
What Happened to the People Who Bought Trading Bots
conflict:retail-trading-bots-not-beat-ma.whyWatch: Bots are the current form of the automatic-income promise and nobody in the corpus has measured one.
conflict:retail-trading-bots-not-beat-ma.tension: Sold as systematic; the only record is an enforcement allegation.
conflict:retail-trading-bots-not-beat-ma.evidenceNeeded: Audited performance of retail bots against a benchmark over a market cycle.
conflict:retail-trading-bots-not-beat-ma.research: Blocked: one FTC allegation about one firm's customers is all the corpus has, and a search on 2026-10-26 found no independent measurement of retail bot users' realised returns against a benchmark: Harke et al. (SSRN 3904097) backtests factor and ML strategies, not bots retail customers bought; the Management Science Yahoo Finance API study measures data access and overconfidence, not bots; bot-vendor figures (e.g. 3Commas user averages) are unaudited self-reports. Unblock with account-level broker or exchange data on retail users of automated or AI trading products (net of fees, over a market cycle, against an index), e.g. a regulator study of algo-tagged retail orders (SEBI Algo-ID) or an exchange's API-bot cohort.
